name: Light Dull Glaucous-Blue
lede: Light Dull Glaucous-Blue is a muted grey-blue from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, filed again by name in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary, and close enough on screen to its own sibling, Light Glaucous-Blue, to be mistaken for it.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone with a near-twin
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate XLII, hue 41″″″, tone d [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary files the exact name "Light Dull Glaucous-Blue" under block 172, "light greenish blue" [2]. The name stacks "light" and "dull" onto [[glaucous-blue]], after the dusty, waxy bloom called glaucous [1].

In our color library its closest neighbor is its own near-twin, [[light-glaucous-blue]], about 3.3 units away, close enough that the two could pass for the same color [3]. [[lumiere-blue]] sits 3.8 units off and greener, and [[pastel-turquoise]] 4.0 units off and darker [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 156 of them, about 0.66 percent, as photographed, more common than 60 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 17 of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 2.1 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 43 percent of its 107 clearly-ranked appearances [4]. Eugène Boudin favors it most, in 5 of his 33 works here, 5.2 times his museums' baseline rate [4]. The earliest dated match is 1475, in a painting by Antonello da Messina, 437 years before the name's first 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of the name's age [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first.
